Contributions

While the existence of these timing side channels is not entirely surprising, especially since these li-

braries do not claim to prevent timing attacks,1 what is striking is how pervasive they are across the DP

libraries we study. As currently implemented, many DP mechanisms could be exploited by an adversary

with access to runtime measurements. In an interactive query system, obtaining such measurements

could be as simple as recording the time between sending a request and receiving a response.

To better assess the risk posed by these side channels, we propose an auditing algorithm that an-

alyzes the joint distribution of a mechanism’s output and runtime (Section 4.3). Our algorithm builds

on the general statistical auditing method of Jagielski, Ullman, and Oprea [JUO20] and yields an em-

pirical lower bound on the privacy parameters when both output and runtime are observable. Using

this auditing algorithm, we show that several of our attacks lead to substantial privacy degradation in

realistic deployment scenarios. Together, these findings suggest that DP libraries should treat timing

attacks as a serious concern in interactive deployments.

We summarize our contributions as follows.

• We investigate timing side channels in the PyDP, diffprivlib, and OpenDP libraries, and identify

vulnerabilities across a range of widely used mechanisms. We show that seemingly innocuous

operations, including filtering, sorting, and multiplication by a constant, can introduce severe

timing side channels that remain observable even in real-world network environments.

• We provide an auditing algorithm for assessing the risk of timing attacks on DP implementa-

tions, and connect this auditing method to the definitional framework for jointly output/timing-

private programs (Chapter 3).

dataset. We assume that the adversary can choose the privacy budget used for each query and can con-

### 4.2 Practical Timing Attacks

In this section, we describe the timing side channels that we identified in the surveyed libraries. We eval-

uate these attacks using two t2.large Amazon AWS instances located in the same region but running

on different physical machines. The average ping latency between the machines was 1.13ms, with a

standard deviation of 0.35ms. Thus, in our experiments, the execution environment includes network

effects such as latency and jitter, shared virtualized cloud hardware resources, and the microarchitec-

tural characteristics of the underlying AWS instances. In this section, our focus is on identifying and

demonstrating these timing side channels. In Section 4.3, we then quantify the resulting privacy degra-

dation using our auditing framework.

To decide which functions to focus on, we looked for components that are widely used in DP

algorithm design and data-processing workflows. In particular, we prioritized transformations and mea-

surements that commonly arise in real-world data analysis pipelines, including filtering, sorting, com-

puting and releasing noisy aggregates such as sums and counts, and private partition selection. These

choices are intended to reflect realistic usage patterns in practical DP systems.

## Attacking Sorting Transformations

We begin with a simple example showing how seemingly innocuous computations can have runtime

distributions that, when observed, lead to clear violations of differential privacy. Consider sorting,

which appears as a subroutine in the DP trimmed mean estimator [BS19] and the smooth-sensitivity

median algorithm [NRS07]. Depending on the sorting algorithm, runtime can vary substantially even

on adjacent datasets. For example, let X = [1, 2, . . . , n] and X′ = [n + 1, n, . . . , 2], which are adja-

cent under the change-one distance metric, since X′ can be obtained from X by replacing the element

1 with n + 1. Running bubble sort on X requires only n −1 comparisons because the input is already

sorted. In contrast, running bubble sort on X′ requires n(n −1)/2 comparisons. Thus, as n grows, the

gap in runtime becomes increasingly pronounced.

To demonstrate a timing side channel arising from sorting, we implemented the DP trimmed

vulnerability could be realized using OpenDP or PyDP. The key point is that the side channel arises

from the sorting subroutine itself, and is therefore independent of the particular DP library used to add

Although this attack may appear contrived because it relies on specially structured inputs, it

illustrates a broader point. Observable timing differences introduced by ordinary data-processing oper-

ations can violate DP guarantees, and these side channels can be adapted to support more targeted at-

tacks. For example, consider an equality-check transformation that maps each record to a bit indicating

whether it matches a target record, such as whether the record belongs to a user Alice. If Alice’s record

appears at the beginning of the dataset, the transformation produces a binary vector with a leading 1

followed by n −1 zeros. If Alice is absent, it produces the all-zero vector. An adversary can then chain

this transformation with a measurement that performs sorting, such as the trimmed mean. The all-zero

vector is already sorted and requires minimal work, while the vector containing a 1 requires additional

comparisons to move that 1 into place. As a result, a small timing difference that depends only on input

order can be amplified into a direct membership inference attack.

mon data-processing operations, including sorting, depends on the order of the input dataset. As a

## Attacking Partition Selection

In many private data analysis tasks, it is necessary to determine which groups or partitions in a dataset

should be included in a release. This decision can itself be sensitive. For example, suppose a medical

researcher at a university conducts a survey of students with a particular health condition and releases

aggregate statistics grouped by nationality. If the output includes a group for a particular nationality,

and only one student at the university has that nationality, then the inclusion of that group may already

reveal that this student participated in the survey and therefore has the health condition. To address

this issue, DP libraries often implement private partition selection mechanisms, which aim to identify

groups in the dataset while preserving privacy.

Both PyDP and OpenDP support private partition selection through a technique known as

Laplace thresholding. At a high level, this method computes the count of each candidate group, adds

Laplace noise with scale 1/ε to each count, and retains only those groups whose noisy counts exceed a

fixed threshold τ. Groups whose noisy counts fall below the threshold are discarded and omitted from

subsequent analysis. In this way, the mechanism attempts to ensure that the decision of whether to in-

clude a group in the output is itself made in a differentially private manner. A pseudocode description

of Laplace thresholding is given in Figure 4.4.

Unfortunately, Laplace thresholding introduces a subtle timing side channel. The total amount

of work performed by the mechanism depends on the number of distinct groups in the dataset, since

it must compute a count, add noise, and compare the noisy count to the threshold for each group. For

example, consider two neighboring datasets X = [A, A] and X′ = [A, B]. On X, the mechanism pro-

cesses only group “A”. On X′, it must process both “A” and “B”, which means that it must perform an

crepancies can be exploited to break DP systems that were specifically designed to prevent timing at-

tacks [HPN11]. In the IEEE floating-point standard, subnormal numbers are nonzero values whose

Finally, while our construction builds on the same basic idea as the attack of Andrysco et al.,

it is arguably more practical and more severe. In their setting, the timing signal depended heavily on

both the dataset size and the position of the target record. In contrast, our attack remains effective on

datasets as small as a single record and is entirely independent of the target’s position. As a result, it can

be scaled to perform full dataset enumeration by iterating over candidate target records and testing for

their presence individually.

## Attacking Filtering Transformations

We now describe an attack on mechanisms that process only a selected subset of their input. As an il-

lustrative example, consider a data analyst querying a healthcare dataset who wants to compute the

number of individuals aged 30 and younger who have a particular disease. A natural way to do this is

to first filter the dataset to retain only rows corresponding to individuals under 30, and then compute a

DP sum over the disease column of the resulting subset.

Unfortunately, this introduces a timing side channel. The runtime of the DP sum in the second

step depends on the size of the filtered dataset produced in the first step. As a result, observing the run-

time can reveal how many records satisfied the filtering predicate, even if the output of the sum itself is

differentially private.

data frames. Specifically, we adapted example code from the OpenDP documentation [Ope25], shown

schematically in Figure 4.11. The mechanism first filters individuals whose usual weekly working hours

## Attacking Randomized Response

Boolean randomized response is one of the most basic and well-known algorithms in the DP toolkit.

It is commonly used in the setting of local DP, where each user runs a randomizer on their own data

### 4.3 Auditing Timing Privacy

In this section, we introduce an auditing technique for estimating lower bounds on a program’s JOT-

DP privacy parameters (Definition 3.1.2, Chapter 3). Concretely, we extend the statistical auditing

framework of Jagielski, Ullman, and Oprea [JUO20] to the joint random variable consisting of both

the program’s output and its execution time. While this extension is conceptually straightforward, it

introduces two additional challenges. First, unlike program outputs,5 runtimes can vary significantly

across execution environments, so empirical probabilities may need to be estimated from environments

whose precise states are unknown or difficult to control. Second, auditing runtime requires choosing a

measurable event in the runtime space. Since runtime measurements are high-resolution and affected

by environmental noise, events that isolate exact runtimes or very small intervals can have little em-

pirical support, leading to unstable estimates and wide confidence intervals. Conversely, events that

aggregate too much of the runtime space can obscure differences between neighboring executions. In

our experiments, we therefore use threshold events that test whether the runtime coordinate exceeds a

chosen threshold τ.

The auditing framework described above is used to assess whether an implementation fails to

satisfy JOT-DP for a given choice of privacy parameters. We make two observations. First, when the

output set π1(O) covers the entire output domain of the program, the audit measures the privacy guar-

antees provided when only the runtime is observable. In many cases, this already suffices to show that a

program does not achieve the desired privacy guarantee, since the runtime distributions on neighboring

inputs can differ substantially.

Second, the observed runtime behavior depends on the execution environment. Ideally, the

environment used for auditing should match the resources and constraints of the production environ-

ment as closely as possible. JOT-DP (Definition 3.3.4, Chapter 3) quantifies privacy over all pairs of

execution environments in a set E. When E is highly restricted, for example if it contains only a single

execution environment,7 it becomes easier to obtain a tight lower bound on the program’s privacy pa-

rameters. In practice, however, the exact execution environment may be difficult to predict, especially

in interactive settings where the system handles many queries and its internal state evolves over time.

For example, a query may place the system in a rare but valid architectural state that induces a severe

### 4.4 Attacks Evaluation

We evaluate our timing attacks using the auditing algorithm from the previous section. Across all ex-

periments, we observe measurable privacy degradation. In many cases, the resulting lower bounds εLB

are far larger than the nominal privacy parameters configured for the mechanism, shown in Table 4.1.

Except for the randomized response experiments, all timing measurements were collected over a net-

work connection, showing that these attacks remain practical in realistic settings. We emphasize that

these mechanisms were configured in the high-privacy regime, with small values of ε, where one would

expect little or no leakage from the outputs alone. However, our audits show that observing runtime

can raise the effective privacy loss well above what the output alone would suggest.

The largest lower bounds arose in our audits of the DP trimmed mean and Lipschitz counting

mechanisms, where we obtained εLB = 6.6 and εLB = 5.9, even though both mechanisms were con-

figured with ε = 0.1. In both cases, the structure of the mechanism allows the side channel to become

arbitrarily severe. For trimmed mean, the timing gap scales with dataset size and row ordering. For Lip-

schitz counting, the adversary can chain together multiple gadgets to amplify the timing difference on

adjacent datasets. Even in the partition selection, filtered sum, and randomized response settings, where

the reported values of εLB are smaller in absolute terms, they still often exceed the configured privacy

parameter by an order of magnitude.

Taken together, these results show that timing attacks are a real concern for practical DP sys-

tems. They arise in ordinary transformations and measurements, and in several cases they lead to effec-

tive privacy loss far larger than one would expect from the output privacy parameters alone.

## Chapter 5

## Pure Timing Privacy in the Unbounded

## Setting

Chapter 3 developed a general technique for constructing timing-private programs. The basic approach

was to bound a program’s timing stability, and then add randomized delay scaled according to that

bound to the program’s execution. However, this approach has two important limitations. First, it in-

herently yields only approximate JOT-DP, even when the original program is pure DP in its output.

Second, it applies only to programs that are timing-stable, and therefore does not apply to computa-

tions with superlinear runtime (Lemma 3.2.11).

These limitations are not prohibitive in the bounded DP setting. When a public bound on

input size is available, one can often obtain pure JOT-DP simply by padding execution to the worst-case

runtime over all inputs within that bound. In the unbounded setting, however, the dataset size itself is

sensitive and may grow arbitrarily large, so this kind of worst-case padding is no longer available.

This chapter studies whether one can nevertheless obtain pure JOT-DP in the unbounded set-

ting while preserving the utility and efficiency of standard DP algorithms as much as possible. A natu-

ral starting point is a result of Ben Dov, David, Naor, and Tzalik [BDDNT23], who showed that pure

DP programs in the unbounded setting can be converted into pure JOT-DP programs. Their result es-

tablished that pure timing privacy is possible in principle, but it left several basic questions unresolved.

In particular, their transformation incurs a constant additive increase in error probability, is computa-

tionally inefficient, and is analyzed in a more restricted model in which runtime is measured only by the

number of random bits used. This leaves open whether, in more standard computational models, one

97


<!-- Page 107 -->


can obtain pure JOT-DP with asymptotically vanishing error and with implementations that remain

efficient.

In this chapter, we address these questions. We show that the achievable utility of pure JOT-

DP in the unbounded setting depends in an essential way on the computational model. In a random-

ized RAM model where the dataset size is given, or can be computed in constant time, and random

numbers can be generated in constant time, one can achieve failure probability that vanishes polyno-

mially with the dataset size. By contrast, if the dataset size is not given, or if the model provides only

a random-bit generator, then an arbitrarily small constant failure probability is the best possible. We

complement these lower bounds with eﬃcient transformations that turn pure JOT-DP programs in the

upper-bounded setting into pure JOT-DP programs in the unbounded setting, while preserving the

original output distribution up to small total variation distance. As corollaries, we obtain pure timing-

private analogues of standard unbounded mechanisms whose accuracy closely matches that of their

non-timing-private counterparts.

## Contributions

We summarize the main contributions of this chapter below.

• We show that pure JOT-DP in the unbounded setting is achievable in the randomized RAM

model, and we give an efficient generic transformation from ε-JOT-DP RAM programs in the

upper-bounded setting to ε′-JOT-DP RAM programs in the unbounded setting for any setting

of ε′ > 2ε. Unlike prior work, the resulting program is explicit and efficient. It makes a single

oracle call to the original upper-bounded program on a truncation of the input, together with

an additional computation whose runtime is linear in the dataset size with high probability. This

gives a general way to lift many useful pure JOT-DP implementations from the upper-bounded

setting to the unbounded one.

• We show that the utility cost of pure JOT-DP in the unbounded setting is inherently model-

dependent. We prove lower bounds showing that every pure JOT-DP program that estimates the

98


<!-- Page 108 -->


input length must incur nontrivial failure probability, and that the best achievable failure prob-

ability depends on the smallest nonzero probabilities that can be sampled within a given time

bound in the underlying computational model. In models where randomness is provided only

by a random-bit generator, constant failure probability is unavoidable. In contrast, in a random-

ized RAM model with access to the input length and constant-time random-number generation,

inverse-polynomial failure probability is achievable.

• We instantiate these general transformations to obtain concrete pure JOT-DP mechanisms in the

unbounded setting. Most notably, we derive a pure JOT-DP analogue of the Laplace mechanism

for releasing sums. Its asymptotic accuracy matches that of the standard unbounded Laplace

mechanism up to constant factors, except that the failure probability decays polynomially rather

than exponentially in the dataset size. Our lower bounds show that this loss is optimal up to con-

stant factors in the RAM model.

## Chapter 6

## Timing Privacy for User-level DP Programs

In this chapter, we consider the user-level setting, where privacy is defined with respect to the addition

or removal of an entire user’s contribution rather than a single record. This setting is natural in appli-

cations where one user may generate many events, such as transactions, searches, clicks, telemetry, or

message metadata. We do not assume that the records contributed by one user appear contiguously in

memory. Instead, a user’s records may be scattered throughout the dataset, interleaved with the records

of many other users. In such settings, protecting only the presence or absence of a single record is often

too weak. The more appropriate goal is to protect whether an entire user’s contribution is present.

Extending the guarantees from Chapter 3 to this setting introduces new difficulties. In that

chapter, we achieved timing privacy by adding randomized delay to programs that are timing-stable,

meaning that their runtime changes by only a bounded amount on adjacent inputs. Under the notion

user-level adjacency (which we denote as dUserID, defined in Definition 2.2.6), however, many natural

user-level algorithms no longer fit this framework, even when each user contributes only a bounded

number of records. When a user’s records may be scattered throughout the input, even simple tasks

such as counting the number of distinct users require tracking which records belong to the same user

while scanning the dataset. Doing this in a timing-stable way is already nontrivial, so many basic user-

level computations fall outside the scope of the framework from Chapter 3.

The problem becomes harder still when there is no a priori bound on the number of records

contributed by a single user. In that regime, adding or removing one user can cause arbitrarily large

changes in runtime, even when the output sensitivity remains bounded. The natural question, then, is

when, and under what assumptions, timing privacy can still be achieved in the user-level setting.

## Motivating Examples

We begin with two basic examples showing why achieving JOT-DP in the user-level setting is not straight-

forward using existing techniques.

Aggregating User Records. Consider a dataset x of transactions collected over time, where each

record contains a user identifier u and a value v ∈[0, b]. Because the records are ordered by time, a

single user’s transactions need not appear contiguously in memory. A basic analytic task is to release the

total transaction value

q(x) = X

(u,v)∈x v

where each record (u, v) of user u contributes a value in v ∈[0, b]. Under user-level adjacency, adding

or removing one user adds or removes all of that user’s transactions. If per-user contributions are un-

bounded, then q has unbounded global sensitivity with respect to dUserID. That is, adding or removing

a single user can change the value of q(x) by an arbitrarily large amount, since one user may contribute

arbitrarily many records.

In the setting where only output privacy is required, the standard remedy is to enforce a per-

user contribution cap. For example, one can truncate x so that each user u contributes at most B trans-

actions, say by keeping only the first B in time order, and then compute q on the truncated dataset.

After this preprocessing step, q has global sensitivity at most B · b with respect to dUserID, so it can be

released using standard DP mechanisms. This truncation may introduce bias when some users con-

tribute more than B records, but that bias is a familiar tradeoff in user-level DP.

However, this approach does not automatically yield JOT-DP. Enforcing a per-user cap re-

quires the algorithm to identify and count each user’s records across the dataset, which in general means

scanning the input and maintaining per-user state, such as counters. If one user contributes far more

than the cap, the algorithm must still process those records in order to identify and discard the excess.

As a result, the runtime can change by an unbounded amount between dUserID-neighboring datasets.

An observer who measures execution time may therefore detect the presence or absence of a heavy con-

tributor even when the output itself is differentially private.

Counting Users. An even simpler example is the task of counting the number of distinct users in

the dataset. From the perspective of output privacy, this query is straightforward. Under user-level ad-

jacency, the number of users has sensitivity 1, since adding or removing one user changes the count by

exactly one. In particular, this query does not require any a priori bound on the number of records con-

tributed by a single user.

From the perspective of timing privacy, however, the picture changes. To count the number

of distinct users, the algorithm must inspect the records in the dataset and maintain a history of which

users have already been seen. The runtime therefore depends on the total number of records that must

be examined, not just on the number of users. If one user contributes many records, then the presence

or absence of that user can substantially change the runtime, creating timing leakage even for a query

with small output sensitivity.

## Contributions

In this work, we initiate the study of JOT-DP (Definition 3.3.4) in the user-level setting, where privacy

is defined with respect to the addition or removal of an entire user’s contribution. We first study the

standard representation in which the input is an arbitrary sequence of user-labeled records. In this de-

fault model, records need not be grouped by user, nor equipped with auxiliary links or indices that re-

veal a user’s contribution structure. We later revisit this modeling choice in Section 6.3, where we show

that preprocessed representations can make some user-level tasks easier from the perspective of timing

privacy. Table 6.1 summarizes the settings considered in this chapter and the corresponding feasibility

results.

The main distinction in the first part of the chapter is therefore the assumption we make about

the size of each user’s contribution. The first case is the bounded-contributions setting, where each user

contributes at most a public constant number of records, but the number of users remains private and

unbounded.

Theorem 6.0.1 (Informal Restatement of Theorem 6.1.1). For any constants ε′ > ε, δ′ > δ, and

β > 0, any (ε, δ)-DP RAM program in the user-level setting in which each user can contribute at most

B ∈N records can be transformed into a (ε′, δ′)-JOT-DP RAM program whose output distribution,

on every input dataset x in which each user contributes at most B records, is β-close in total variation

distance to that of the original program on x.

In contrast, when per-user contributions are unbounded, timing privacy imposes a much

stronger barrier. We prove that no algorithm can achieve even approximate JOT-DP while retaining

nontrivial utility in full generality. This obstruction already appears for basic tasks such as counting

users, but our impossibility result is more general. It applies to arbitrary target queries and continues to

hold even in a promise setting where privacy must hold on all datasets, but accuracy is required only on

well-behaved datasets in which each user contributes at most a bounded number of records.

Theorem 6.0.2 (Informal Restatement of Theorem 6.2.1). Fix any bound k ∈N and let Goodk de-

note the class of datasets in which every user contributes at most k records. Even if accuracy is required

128


<!-- Page 138 -->


only on datasets in Goodk, any (ε, δ)-JOT-DP RAM program whose privacy guarantee must hold on

all datasets must incur large error on some dataset in Goodk whenever the target query has unbounded

range on Goodk.

Thus, without additional assumptions on the input domain, one cannot in general hope to ob-

tain useful user-level JOT-DP algorithms in the unbounded-contributions setting. More broadly, this

also yields a separation from the output-only setting. Unlike in the pure output-only DP setting, where

private algorithms can always be extended from a restricted domain to the full domain [BCSZ18],

timing-private programs cannot always be extended from a well-behaved subclass to the full domain

while preserving useful behavior on that subclass (Corollary 6.2.3).

We then show that this impossibility can be circumvented under a different type of assump-

tion, namely a natural restricted-domain assumption that rules out datasets dominated by a single user.

In particular, we consider the domain Xγ of γ-balanced datasets, where each user contributes at most a

constant fraction of the total number of records. For this domain, we construct approximate JOT-DP

programs by reducing to the upper-bounded setting, where a public upper bound on the input size is

known in advance. Concretely, we show how to transform any timing-private algorithm for that upper-

bounded setting into one for the unbounded setting that remains accurate on Xγ. The resulting pro-

gram satisfies (ε, δ)-JOT-DP with respect to dUserID-adjacency restricted to Xγ, meaning that privacy is

required only over adjacent pairs x, x′ ∈Xγ. Moreover, its output distribution remains within a small

constant β in total variation distance of that of the original upper-bounded algorithm.

denote the space of datasets in which each user contributes at most a γ-fraction of the total number of

records. For any (ε, δ)-JOT-DP RAM program with respect to dUserID in the upper-bounded setting,

and for any ε′ > ε, δ′ > δ, and β > 0, there exists a compiler that transforms the program into

Finally, we consider the case where the DP computation observed by the adversary is not run

on an arbitrary sequence of records. Instead, we assume that the input has already been preprocessed, in

a step unobservable to the adversary, so that records are grouped by user identifier. This is a stronger as-

sumption than the one used in our preceding results, since the preprocessing step itself may have data-

dependent runtime. Under this assumption, the observed program can access each user’s contribution

as a contiguous block.

Theorem 6.0.4 (Informal Restatement of Theorem 6.3.5). Suppose the input has been preprocessed,

in a step unobservable to the adversary, so that records are grouped by user identifier. Also suppose

there is a public per-user contribution bound B. Then, for any chosen truncation cap b ≤B, user-level

DP computations that first keep only the first b records from each user and then run a DP computation

on the truncated dataset can be implemented as JOT-DP RAM programs whose observable runtime

scales with the number of users and the chosen cap b, rather than with the worst-case bound B.

This distinction is important in practice. A public bound B may be extremely loose, while the

analyst may only want to retain the first b ≪B records per user. In an arbitrary input order, enforc-

ing such a cap can require searching through the whole dataset to find all records belonging to the same

user. In the grouped representation, the observed computation can instead process each user block lo-

cally, keep only the first b records, and then run the desired DP computation on the truncated dataset.

Taken together, these results clarify when JOT-DP is achievable in the user-level setting. With-

out additional assumptions, accurate timing-private computation cannot be achieved in general when

per-user contributions are unbounded. Positive results become possible once one assumes a bound

on each user’s contribution, restricts attention to datasets in which no user dominates the input, or

changes the input representation so that each user’s contribution structure is directly accessible.

Beyond their theoretical interest, our results also provide guidance for practitioners designing

user-level DP systems. They identify which input assumptions make timing privacy feasible, when tim-

ing leakage is unavoidable, and when preprocessing or data layout can materially simplify the problem.

More broadly, they provide the first general constructions of efficient user-level DP programs that are

also resistant to timing attacks and that closely match the accuracy of their non-timing-private counter-

parts.

### 6.1 Bounded User-Contributions Setting

We begin with the bounded-contributions regime, in which each user may contribute at most B ∈N

records to the dataset. This assumption limits how much any one user can affect both the output and

the runtime of an algorithm. In many common algorithms, runtime is a monotone function of the

total number of records processed. Thus, if each user contributes at most B records and the total num-

ber of users is public information, as in the bounded-DP setting, then the total number of records is

bounded in advance by B times that user bound. In that case, we can pad every execution to the worst-

case runtime for inputs of the maximum possible size.

The more interesting case is when the number of users is unbounded. Even in this setting,

many common data-processing algorithms are timing-stable with respect to dUserID when per-user

contributions are bounded. This includes algorithms whose runtime is linear in the total number of

records and that perform only bounded work per record. For such algorithms, changing one user’s

data changes the runtime by only a bounded amount. As a result, Theorem 3.5.5 applies directly once

the input metric is instantiated as dUserID. Still, timing-stable programs necessarily have O(n) run-

time [RV24], which rules out many natural data-analysis tasks. For example, even counting the number

of users in a dataset may require hashing or sorting user identifiers, and such computations need not be

timing-stable with respect to dUserID.

Nevertheless, when per-user contributions are bounded a priori, we can still achieve JOT-DP

for arbitrary user-level DP computations. At a high level, we first privately compute a size bound U

that, with high probability, is at least the input length. If |x| ≤U, the compiled program runs the

original DP program on x and pads the execution to the worst-case runtime of the original program on

inputs of length at most U. If |x| > U, the compiled program instead runs the original DP program on

the empty dataset. On the high-probability event that the private bound is large enough, the fallback

branch is not used, so the output distribution agrees with that of the original program. Moreover, on

this event, the observable runtime is determined by the private bound U rather than by the exact input

length. The probability that U underestimates the input length is charged to the approximate privacy

parameter, yielding an approximately JOT-DP compiler.

### 6.2 The Unbounded Contributions Setting

The positive results of Section 6.1 rely on the assumption that per-user contributions are bounded a

priori. When this assumption is removed, the situation changes fundamentally. In the unbounded-

contributions setting, timing privacy severely limits what can be computed, even for the simplest user-

level statistics. In particular, we show that no (ε, δ)-JOT-DP algorithm can achieve nontrivial accuracy

on all datasets, even when accuracy is only required on well-behaved inputs.

At a high level, the impossibility arises because a single heavy-contributing user can dominate

the dataset. When per-user contributions are unbounded, it is possible to construct datasets in which,

with high probability, a timing-private algorithm observes only records belonging to one user before

halting. Joint output/timing privacy then requires that the joint distribution of outputs and run-

times on such a dataset be close to that on a neighboring dataset in which that user is removed. As a

result, the algorithm’s output distribution must be nearly the same on datasets with many users and on

datasets with only one, precluding accurate estimation of queries whose value depends on the number

or diversity of users.

## Privacy for γ-Balanced Datasets

Impossibility results in the unbounded-contributions setting are driven by the fact that a neighboring

dataset may differ by a user whose contribution is so large that it can dominate the computation and

radically change the runtime distribution.

We therefore study a relaxed setting in which no single user can dominate the dataset. Con-

cretely, we restrict attention to balanced datasets, where every user contributes at most a γ-fraction of

the records, for γ ∈(0, 1). We keep the standard user-level insert/delete distance dUserID, but require

the JOT-DP guarantee only for adjacent pairs that remain within the balanced class.

### 6.3 Preprocessed Datasets

The impossibility result of Theorem 6.2.1 is partly driven by the input representation. Throughout this

paper, we model inputs as arbitrary sequences of user-labeled records. It is therefore natural to ask what

changes if the dataset is instead stored in a representation that is more aligned with user-level computa-

tion. In this section, we consider a different kind of relaxation, in which the dataset is first transformed

by a one-time preprocessing step that is not observable to the adversary.

A canonical preprocessing step is to group the records by user identifier, so that all records con-

tributed by the same user appear contiguously in memory. Once the input has this structure, tasks such

as counting users or truncating each user’s contribution become much more tractable from the per-

spective of timing privacy. The reason is that the computation no longer needs to recover a user’s con-

tribution from an arbitrary interleaving of records. Instead, each user’s contribution appears as a single

contiguous block, so once the program reaches the beginning of that block, it can process only the por-

tion it needs and then move directly to the next user.

A particularly convenient representation is one in which the first record of each user’s block

stores auxiliary metadata giving the size of that block.

Definition 6.3.1 (Grouped and length-annotated grouped representations). A dataset x ∈X is in

grouped form if all records contributed by the same user appear contiguously in memory.

149


<!-- Page 159 -->


We say that x is in length-annotated grouped form if x is in grouped form and, in addition, the

representation stores the length of each user’s block with the first record of that block.

Under this stronger assumption of a dataset being in length-annotated grouped form, after read-

ing the first B records of a user’s block, the program can immediately jump to the next block. Thus

many natural user-level preprocessing tasks become timing-stable on the already-preprocessed repre-

sentation. For example, user counting becomes O(1)-timing-stable (Lemma 6.3.2), and truncating each

user to their first B records becomes O(B)-timing-stable (Lemma 6.3.3).

Lemma 6.3.2 (User counting is O(1)-timing-stable on length-annotated grouped-by-user inputs).

Fix the user-level insert-delete relation dID-USER. Let Pcount be the RAM program that, on an input

in length-annotated grouped-by-user form, counts the number of users by reading the first record of

each user block and jumping directly to the next block using the stored block length. Then Pcount is

O(1)-timing-stable with respect to dID-USER.

Proof. Let x, x′ be adjacent datasets, so x′ is obtained from x by inserting or deleting all records of a

single user. Because the input is in length-annotated grouped-by-user form, the program processes the

dataset block by block. On each block, it performs a fixed amount of work: it reads the first record,

increments a counter, reads the stored block length, and jumps to the first record of the next block.

Passing from x to x′ changes the representation by at most one user block. Thus the executions

of Pcount on x and x′ differ by only one iteration of this fixed-cost loop. Therefore the runtime changes

by at most a constant, so Pcount is O(1)-timing-stable.

## Chapter 7

## Conclusion

This thesis developed foundations for reasoning about differential privacy in the presence of timing

side channels. Standard definitions of differential privacy protect only the released output of an algo-

rithm, but real implementations may also reveal runtime. To account for this threat, we studied joint

output/timing privacy, treating mechanisms as programs in a computational model whose output

and runtime are both observable. We then developed stability notions for analyzing runtime leakage,

showed how randomized delay can transform timing-stable programs into timing-private programs,

and gave chaining and composition tools for reasoning about more complex computations.

We also showed that timing side channels arise in real implementations of differential privacy.

Through attacks on OpenDP, PyDP, and diffprivlib, we demonstrated that common operations such

as filtering, sorting, private partition selection, floating-point multiplication, and randomized response

can leak sensitive information through runtime. These attacks show that timing leakage is a practical

concern for deployed DP systems, not just a pathology of toy examples. They also motivate treating

runtime as part of the observable behavior of a DP implementation, rather than as an implementation

detail outside the privacy analysis.

Finally, we studied when timing privacy can and cannot be achieved. In the unbounded setting,

where dataset size is sensitive, we gave efficient constructions of pure JOT-DP programs and proved

lower bounds showing that the achievable error depends on the computational model. In the user-level

setting, we showed that bounded per-user contributions allow ordinary user-level DP programs to be

compiled into JOT-DP programs, while unbounded per-user contributions lead to strong impossibility

results. Taken together, these results show that timing behavior is a fundamental part of the privacy in-

155


<!-- Page 165 -->


terface of differentially private systems. They also show that, under appropriate structural assumptions,

DP implementations can be designed so that their observable behavior more faithfully matches their

formal privacy guarantees.
